| Language   | Performance                                      | Learning Curve                            | Ecosystem                                          |
|------------|--------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| **Python**  | Slow (CPython GIL); fine for small tools, not CPU-bound | Very low — readable, dynamic, forgiving    | Vast (PyPI), batteries-included stdlib             |
| **Rust**    | Very fast — zero-cost abstractions, no runtime   | Steep — borrow checker, ownership model   | Strong (crates.io), but fewer beginner-friendly libs for CLI glue |
| **Go**      | Fast — compiled, no GC pauses like CPython       | Low-to-moderate — simple syntax, static typing is straightforward | Mature (stdlib is excellent for CLI), fewer niche crates than PyPI/crates.io |
| **TypeScript** | Moderate — JS engine overhead; not CPU-bound friendly  | Low-to-moderate — familiar syntax, type system takes some getting used to if new to TS | Large (npm), but much of it is web-focused; Node ecosystem can be noisy with dead packages |

**TL;DR for a small CLI tool:**

- If you want speed and simplicity: **Python** or Go**. Python if it's purely glue/data-parsing and doesn't need to be fast. Go if you need compiled-binary distribution and reasonable performance.
- If performance is critical (e.g. heavy computation): **Rust**, well... **Rust**. I mean — Rust. But the learning curve will cost time upfront.
- If the tool lives in a Node/TS environment anyway: **TypeScript** makes sense for reuse of existing patterns and shared types.**

No, there's no single dedicated regulation yet, but the European Commission is actively working on it:

- **AI Agents Regulation (2026)** — The Commission proposed this in January 2026 alongside the AI Act. It specifically targets autonomous AI agents that acts on behalf of natural persons (chatbots, autonomous services, etc.). Status as of July 2026: the proposal entered the European Parliament's internal review process (the formal legislative procedure hasn't started yet). The text is publicly available at eur-lex.europa.eu.

- **AI Act** — Already in force (passed in 2024, phased into effect starting August 1 2026). It doesn't cover "AI agents" specifically but sets risk categories for all AI systems (from prohibited uses to general-purpose AI obligations). Many obligations for high-risk systems and foundation models are already effective as of summer 20.

The status is:
| Regulation | Stage | When effective |
|---|---|---|
| AI Act | In force | Phased 201/8/–end of 2 |
| AI Agents Reg. Proposal | Proposed by Commission (Jan 2) | Not yet — requires Parliament + Council adoption, expected 1– years more |

So it's coming — the proposal is out, but it's not law yet. The timeline depends on how fast the co-legislators move; expect at least another year or two before enactment, with member states then having a further implementation window.

## What Hermes Agent Already Supports Today

Hermes Agent **already has native voice** — it works over **Discord voice channels**. Here's what it does today:

**The current voice pipeline:**
- You join a Discord voice channel
- You speak → Discord sends audio → Hermes's local **faster-whisper** (on this machine) transcribes it instantly
- Hermes processes your message → generates a text reply → calls **text-to-speech** (via your configured provider: Edge TTS, OpenAI TTS, etc.) → plays the audio back in the same Discord channel

**Real-time interruption:** Yes — if you speak while Hermes is talking, the new audio overrides its response mid-turn. That's how Discord turn-based voice works natively.

So right now, to get Grok-like voice conversation, you:
1. **Join a Discord voice channel** that has Hermes connected as a bot
2. **Speak naturally** — ask questions, interrupt when it finishes answering; interrupt it mid-sentence just by starting to talk (it detects your input and stops speaking)

This is essentially the same flow as Grok or ChatGPT voice — speak, get spoken response, interrupt freely. The latency is low because transcription and LLM inference are local on this machine. One small difference: in ChatGPT Voice, they stream audio back to you so you can start hearing while they're still generating — that reduces perceived latency for long answers. Hermes batches TTS at the end of each turn so there's a short pause before you hear any audio for longer responses. That's not yet streamed TTS (a future enhancement).

**Want to try it now?**
- Join one of the Discord channels where I'm present (I'm already connected to Discord via the bot token)
